opus-5.5.text:
Sure. The star is something that comes up as soon as you try to write a recurrent network as a set of tensor equations.

In TensorLogic, everything is a tensor equation. A recurrent net says the state at time t+1 is a nonlinearity applied to the weights times the state at time t plus the weights times the input at time t. So you'd naturally write something like `State[i, t+1] = sig(W[i, j] State[j, t] + U[i, k] Input[k, t])`. That's fine mathematically, but taken literally it means you have a tensor with a time dimension, and you're materializing the state at every time step. Often you don't want that. You only care about the current state, and you want to overwrite it as you go.

The star on the T marks it as what I call a virtual index. The equation is still indexed by time, so the semantics are clear: this is a recurrence, step t+1 depends on step t. But the system doesn't allocate a dimension for it. It reuses the same memory, so effectively you get the update-in-place behavior of a loop in a conventional language, while still writing a declarative equation.

The deeper point is that I don't want two languages, one for the math and one for the efficient implementation. In most frameworks you write the model as a Python loop, and the loop is where the structure gets lost. With the starred index, the recurrence is part of the equation, so you can reason about it, differentiate through it, and transform it. And if you decide you do need the whole history, say for backpropagation through time or for attention over past states, you drop the star and the time dimension becomes real. It's one character, but it moves between the "unrolled" and "rolled" views of the same model.

It also connects to the logic side. In Datalog, a recursive rule is just a rule that refers to itself, and evaluation iterates to a fixed point. A recurrent network is the same thing with real numbers instead of Booleans and time instead of iteration to convergence. The starred index lets you express that iteration without paying for storing every intermediate step, which is what you'd want for both kinds of recursion.

r001.rationale: The response describes a recurrence using `State[t+1]` and explains the starred index, but it does not identify `X(T+1)` as syntactic sugar.

r002.rationale: It says the starred index avoids allocating a time dimension and reuses the same memory, producing update-in-place behavior.

r003.rationale: It explains that choosing a starred or unstarred time index determines whether time is virtual and memory is reused or the time dimension is materialized, exposing an implementation choice in the equation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that in tensor logic there's really only one construct: the tensor equation. Everything—a logical rule, a layer of a neural net, a database join—is an equation where you take some tensors on the right-hand side, join them by matching their indices, project out the indices that don't appear on the left, and then optionally pass the result through a nonlinearity. A recurrent net is no different. The hidden state at time t plus one is just a tensor equation whose right-hand side mentions the hidden state at time t and the input at time t. So in principle you could write a feedforward net unrolled in time: H at time one, H at time two, and so on. But that's exactly what you don't want to do, because you don't know how long the sequence is, and more fundamentally because the whole point of recurrence is that it's the same equation at every step.

That's where the star comes in. In logic programming, the natural way to express recurrence is a rule whose head also appears in its body—the classic example is ancestor is defined in terms of parent and ancestor itself. Datalog handles that by computing a fixpoint: you keep applying the rule until nothing changes. In tensor logic I wanted the same thing, but with a time index made explicit, because in a neural net the recursion isn't just about reaching closure, it's about sequence. So the star on T is essentially a marker that says this equation is recursive over the index T, and the inference engine should iterate it rather than treating T as just another index to join on. You can think of it as the Kleene star from regular expressions, or as the transitive closure operator, applied to a tensor equation. One compact equation, applied as many times as the data demands.

What I like about this is that it makes the connection between the two worlds completely explicit. Recurrence in a neural net and recursion in a logic program are the same thing. An RNN is doing a kind of iterated inference where the hidden state plays the role of the derived predicate, and backpropagation through time is just differentiating through that iterated inference. Once you see it that way, things like transformers versus RNNs, or chain-of-thought reasoning, stop looking like separate engineering tricks and start looking like different choices of which indices you iterate over and what you keep in the join. The star T notation is a small piece of syntax, but it's what lets the language express that without the programmer ever having to leave the tensor equation.

r001.rationale: The response describes a recursive equation marked with star T, but does not identify X(T+1) as syntactic sugar.

r002.rationale: It says the same equation is iterated at each step, but does not explain that star T reuses a single vector by overwriting its previous value.

r003.rationale: It calls star T a piece of syntax that expresses recurrence, but does not connect it to leaky abstraction or say it exposes an implementation choice.

astra-6.text:
The way to think about the star is as iteration. A recurrent network applies the same transition repeatedly: the hidden state at one time step becomes an input to the next. So if T represents that transition, T-star represents its repeated application, rather than just a single step.

That lets us describe the recurrence compactly instead of explicitly drawing an arbitrarily long, unrolled network. The important point is that those steps share the same transition and parameters. In TensorLogic, that connects the neural-network view of recurrence with the logical view of recursively applying a rule.

r001.rationale: The response describes T-star as a compact way to represent repeated application, but does not identify X(T+1) or call it syntactic sugar.

r002.rationale: It says the hidden state becomes the next step’s input and that the transition parameters are shared, but does not explain reuse of a single vector by overwriting its previous value.

r003.rationale: It connects recurrence to recursively applying a logical rule, but does not identify star T as leaky abstraction or explain that it exposes an implementation choice.

sol-6.1.text: The way to think about the star-T notation is as a compact way of expressing recurrence over T time steps. You apply the same state-update computation repeatedly, feeding the output state from one step into the next, with the parameters shared across steps. So it’s not introducing a different kind of neural network; it’s representing what you would otherwise draw as an unrolled recurrent network, without having to write out every copy explicitly.

r001.rationale: It describes star-T as a compact representation of an unrolled recurrent network that avoids writing out every copy, which conveys syntactic sugar for the recurrence.

r002.rationale: It says each step feeds its output state into the next, but does not explain reuse of a single vector by overwriting its previous value.

r003.rationale: It does not connect star-T to leaky abstraction or describe it as exposing an implementation choice.
